title: Ottoman vocabulary
seoTitle: Ottoman Turkish words and their modern pairs
intro: A century ago, written Turkish took a large part of its vocabulary from Arabic and Persian. The language reform of the 1930s replaced many of those words with Turkish ones, but the Ottoman layer never disappeared: it lives on in pairs such as *cevap* and *yanıt*, in the language of history and law, and in words that today sound formal, old-fashioned or ironic. This unit teaches you to read that layer: to know a word's modern partner, to place it in its world, to hear what it adds to a sentence, and to read Ottoman Turkish in Latin letters. The grammar inside these words, the izafet and the Arabic plurals, was the subject of [C1 unit 4](c1-u04-grammar); this guide is about the words themselves.

sections.title: Two words for one thing: Ottoman and Öz Türkçe pairs

blocks.text: From 1932 on, the Turkish Language Association looked for Turkish words to replace Arabic and Persian ones (see the [interlude](c2-u03-culture)). The words it found or coined are called *öz Türkçe* (Turkish proper, native Turkish); the language they were meant to replace is *Osmanlıca*, Ottoman Turkish. Ninety years later, a pair can have ended in one of three ways: the new word won, the old one won, or both stayed, each with its own tone.

blocks.caption: Pairs and how they ended
head: Ottoman word
Öz Türkçe word
Today
rows: *okul* won; TDK marks *mektep* as old-fashioned, and it survives in names and memories
*öğrenci* won; TDK sends *talebe* to *öğrenci*, and it sounds dated
*sözlük* won; TDK sends *lügat* to *sözlük*, and marks its other old sense, **word**, as old-fashioned
*sınav* won for exams; *imtihan* keeps a figurative sense, a trial or ordeal
both alive: *cevap* is the everyday word, *yanıt* a little more written
both alive and neutral; *sözcük* is the usual term in grammar books
both alive; *mesele* also means **the point, the thing**: *Mesele şu.*
both alive; *özgürlük* is the everyday word, *hürriyet* sounds historical or solemn
*doğa* is the usual word for nature; *tabiat* also means **temperament**

blocks.text: **Reading the dictionary.** TDK's online dictionary (*Güncel Türkçe Sözlük*) shows these choices with two marks. An arrow, ►, sends you from a word to the one TDK prefers: *talebe* ► *öğrenci*, *hürriyet* ► *özgürlük*. The label *esk.* (*eskimiş*, old-fashioned) marks a word or a sense that has fallen out of use: *sual*, *tayyare*, *mektep*. An arrow alone is not a ban: *mesele* ► *sorun*, yet *mesele* is heard every day.

**Meaning shifts.** Not every new word settled where it was aimed. *Sorun* was first proposed for Ottoman words meaning **demand** and **affairs**, and ended up as the partner of *mesele*; the word proposed for *mesele* itself, *sorum*, never caught on. For *tayyare* the lists offered *uçkan*, but speakers chose *uçak*. For *akıl* (reason) the 1930s lists gave twenty-eight candidates, and *akıl* is still the word. A pair is decided by speakers, not by a committee.

items.en: My grandfather still calls school mektep.
The thing is, nobody is answering.

items.tr: Bu hastalık bütün aile için ağır bir imtihan oldu.
items.seg: Bu hastalık bütün aile için ağır bir imtihan ol|du.
items.en: This illness was a heavy trial for the whole family.

items.tr: Sorunuza en geç bir hafta içinde yazılı olarak yanıt verilecektir.
items.seg: Soru|nuz|a en geç bir hafta için|de yazılı olarak yanıt ver|il|ecek|tir.
items.en: Your question will be answered in writing within a week at the latest.

items.tr: Kardeşimin tabiatı çok sakindir; kolay kolay sinirlenmez.
items.seg: Kardeş|im|in tabiat|ı çok sakin|dir; kolay kolay sinirlen|mez.

blocks.text: Old-fashioned is not wrong. You will meet *talebe*, *sual* and *lügat* in novels, in the speech of older people and in names. What sounds odd is mixing them into a modern sentence without a reason: *Sualimi anladın mı?* in a text message sounds like a joke, or like your great-grandfather.

English readers know the effect from pairs like **begin** and **commence**, or **ask** and **inquire**: one word from the old core, one borrowed, and the same meaning with a different weight. Turkish pairs work the other way round: the borrowed word is usually the older, heavier one.

sections.title: The words of the Ottoman world: state, law and household

blocks.text: History books, historical novels and the many Ottoman-era television series share a vocabulary of their own. Most of it names things that no longer exist, so it has no modern partner: you simply learn it, as you would *knight* or *duke* in English.

blocks.caption: The state
head: Word
Meaning
Note
rows: also *sultan*; in folk tales, a king ([A2 unit 2](a2-u02))
grand vizier, head of the government
also *veziriazam*; TDK: **prime minister in the Ottoman state**
the sadrazam was the first of the viziers
pasha, the title of high officials and generals

*Divan-ı Hümayun*; *divan* is also a sofa, and a poet's collected poems ([C1 unit 4](c1-u04-culture))
figuratively, an order: *ölüm fermanı*, a death warrant

Meaning

still the official word; *yargıç* is its Öz Türkçe partner, and both are used

blocks.text: Legal language changes slowly, so it kept much of the Ottoman layer. A contract still opens with *işbu* (this), a lawyer's client is a *müvekkil*, a power of attorney is a *vekâletname*, and the court's paper that reaches you is a *tebligat* (section 3).

**Household and family.** Ottoman-era novels and older speakers use Arabic and Persian words where you would say *baba*, *anne* and *ev*: *peder* (father), *valide* (mother, also in the title *Valide Sultan*, the sultan's mother) and *hane* (house, household). Some live on in fixed uses. *Pederim* is playfully formal today. *Hane* is how a village counts its homes (*Köyde kırk hane var*, there are forty households in the village), and it is the Persian ending of *kahvehane* and *kütüphane* ([C1 unit 4](gp-persian-affixes)), shortened to *-ane* in *eczane*, *postane* and *hastane*.

items.en: The grand vizier read out the sultan's edict.

items.tr: Kadı iki tarafı da dinledi ve hükmünü verdi.
items.seg: Kadı iki taraf|ı da dinle|di ve hükm|ü|n|ü ver|di.

items.tr: Mahkeme, tanığın ifadesini dinledikten sonra kararını açıkladı.
items.seg: Mahkeme, tanığ|ın ifade|s|i|n|i dinle|dik|ten sonra karar|ı|n|ı açıkla|dı.

The title deed of this house is in my grandfather's name.

blocks.text: Ottoman titles in today's life: *paşa* is still the word for a general, *bey*, *hanım* and *efendi*, once marks of rank, are ordinary words of address ([A1 unit 3](a1-u03)), and *Valide Sultan* and *sadrazam* are household words thanks to historical series.
*Vakıf* (foundation) and *vâkıf* (aware of, knowing) are two different words, told apart only by the circumflex. In a modern text you will almost always meet the first.

sections.title: What an Ottoman word signals today

blocks.text: When a speaker could say *izin* but says *müsaade*, or writes *işbu* instead of *bu*, the choice tells you something. The meaning stays; the speaker you seem to be changes. Five effects are common.

blocks.caption: Five effects of an Ottoman word
head: Effect
Examples
Where you meet it
rows: *müsaadenizle* (with your permission), *arz ederim* (I respectfully submit), *hâlihazırda* (at present)
the vocabulary of religious life is mostly Arabic, and these words have no Öz Türkçe partners in common use
*mektep*, *muallim*, *kıraathane* (an old-style coffeehouse with newspapers), *eczahane* on an old sign
memoirs, old shop signs, period films
*zatıalileri* (his or her excellency), *teşrif etmek* (to honour with one's presence), *binaenaleyh* (consequently), *mütemadiyen* (continually)

blocks.text: **Formality.** In a meeting or a letter, an Ottoman word raises the tone without sounding odd: *Müsaadenizle, bir şey eklemek istiyorum* is simply polite. TDK still lists *hâlihazırda* as an ordinary adverb; it belongs in notices and reports. Words that TDK marks as old-fashioned, such as *mezkûr*, are best left to the documents where you find them.

**Irony.** Because these words are grand, using them for small things is funny. When a friend arrives an hour late, someone may announce *Zatıalileri nihayet teşrif ettiler!*, His Excellency has finally deigned to come, with the plural of respect on the verb. TDK's own example for *teşrif etmek* is ironic in the same way. *Binaenaleyh* in a message about who pays for dinner is a joke about sounding like a 19th-century official.

items.en: With your permission, let's end the meeting here.
This contract has been signed today.
His Excellency has finally deigned to join us!
items.note: Said with a smile about someone who is late.

items.tr: Mahallemizde eski bir kıraathane var; dedem orada gazete okurdu.
items.seg: Mahalle|miz|de eski bir kıraathane var; dede|m ora|da gazete oku|r|du.
items.en: There's an old coffeehouse in our neighbourhood; my grandfather used to read the paper there.

items.tr: Pizza bitti; binaenaleyh akşam yemeğini sen ısmarlıyorsun.
items.seg: Pizza bit|ti; binaenaleyh akşam yemeğ|i|n|i sen ısmarl|ıyor|sun.
items.en: The pizza is gone; consequently, dinner is on you.
items.note: A joke: an official's word for a small conclusion.

blocks.text: To hear the effect, swap the word: *müsaadenizle* / *izninizle*, *mütemadiyen* / *sürekli*, *binaenaleyh* / *bu yüzden*, *hâlihazırda* / *şu anda*. What changes is not the meaning but the voice.
Used without intent, an Ottoman word can sound like a mistake rather than a style. In everyday messages, prefer the everyday word, and keep the grand one for when you mean the effect.

sections.title: Reading Ottoman Turkish in Latin letters

blocks.text: Ottoman Turkish was written in the Arabic script until 1928 ([A1 unit 1](a1-u01-culture)). Today most readers meet Ottoman texts in Latin letters, in one of three forms. Telling them apart, and reading the marks of the first two, opens the literature and the documents of the 19th century to you.

blocks.caption: Three ways an Ottoman text reaches you
head: Form
Example
What it does
rows: long vowels with a macron, Arabic consonants with dots, `ʿ` and `ʾ` for the Arabic ayn and hemze: the original spelling can be recovered letter by letter
long vowels with a circumflex, an apostrophe for ayn and hemze, the izafet with a hyphen: the author's words, readable without training
the text rewritten in today's words: easy to read, but no longer the author's language

blocks.text: **The marks.** A circumflex usually marks a long vowel: *Kânûn* is read with two long vowels. After k, g or l it may instead mark the soft, palatal consonant you know from *kâğıt* and *dükkân*. An apostrophe inside a word stands for ayn or hemze, two Arabic consonants that Turkish doesn't pronounce as consonants: *san'at*, *mes'ele*, *ma'lûm*. Modern spelling drops most of these marks (*sanat*, *mesele*, *malum*), but TDK's dictionary still gives each word's source in scholarly form: next to *mesele* it writes `Arapça mesʾele`, next to *talebe* `Arapça ṭalebe`.

**Izafet chains** ([C1 unit 4](gp-persian-izafet)) are written with a hyphen, `-ı`/`-i` after a consonant and `-yı`/`-yi` after a vowel: *Dîvân-ı Hümâyûn* (the Imperial Council), *Kuvâ-yı Milliye* (the National Forces). The head comes first, as with English **of**: *Takvîm-i Vekâyi'* is the calendar of events, *Tercümân-ı Ahvâl* the interpreter of conditions, the reverse of a Turkish compound such as *olaylar takvimi*. The Persian **and** is a separate *u* or *ü*, *vü* after a vowel: *Hüsn ü Aşk* (Beauty and Love), Şeyh Gâlib's long poem of the 1780s.

**Old spellings of Turkish words.** Transcriptions of older texts keep forms that modern Turkish has changed: *içün* for *için*, *-ub* or *-üb* for `-(y)Ip` (*alub*, *gelüb*), *dahi* for *de*, *eylemek* for *etmek*, *olmağa* for *olmaya*, and the copula written apart, *idi* and *imiş* ([C2 unit 2](gp-literary-forms)).

**One sentence, two centuries.** Before the reform, Turkish schoolbooks stated the area of a triangle like this: almost every content word is Arabic, and the sentence holds two izafets. Below it is the same rule in modern terms, as the 1937 booklet *Geometri*, which gave Turkish words such as *üçgen*, *açı* and *çarpım*, put it.

items.tr: Bir müsellesin mesaha-i sathiyyesi, kaidesiyle irtifaının hâsıl-ı darbının nısfına müsavidir.
items.en: The surface area of a triangle is equal to half the product of its base and its height.
items.note: The Ottoman textbook wording, as Şükrü Haluk Akalın quotes it.

items.tr: Bir üçgenin alanı, tabanı ile yüksekliğinin çarpımının yarısına eşittir.
items.seg: Bir üçgen|in alan|ı, taban|ı ile yüksekliğ|i|n|in çarpım|ı|n|ın yarı|s|ı|n|a eşit|tir.
items.en: The area of a triangle is equal to half the product of its base and its height.

blocks.text: **Dates.** Ottoman documents count years from the Hijra (*hicri*), and editions often give both calendars: *h. 1247 / m. 1831*, where *m.* stands for *miladi*, of the Christian era. Hijri years are lunar, so one hijri year spans parts of two of ours.
Transcriptions differ from edition to edition: *Takvîm-i Vekâyi'*, *Takvim-i Vekayi* and `Taḳvīm-i Veḳāyiʿ` are the same newspaper. To search a library catalogue, type the title without its marks.

In a bookshop, look at the cover and the foreword. *Sadeleştiren* (simplified by) means the text was rewritten in modern words; an edition that keeps the author's words usually says so in its foreword, and often adds a glossary at the back.

summary: Many Ottoman words have an Öz Türkçe partner: some lost (*mektep*, *sual*, *tayyare*), some share the work with a different tone (*cevap* / *yanıt*, *mesele* / *sorun*).
In TDK's dictionary, ► points to the preferred word and *esk.* marks an old-fashioned one.
The words of the Ottoman state and household (*sadrazam*, *ferman*, *kadı*, *peder*, *valide*, *hane*) name a world that has gone, so they have no partner.
Law keeps much of its older vocabulary: *hâkim* beside *yargıç*, *vakıf*, *işbu*, *vekâletname*.
An Ottoman word can make a sentence formal (*müsaadenizle*), legal (*işbu*), nostalgic (*mektep*) or ironic (*Zatıalileri teşrif ettiler*).
Transcriptions mark long vowels with â, î and û, ayn and hemze with an apostrophe, and the izafet with a hyphen: *Kânûn-ı Esâsî*.
A *sadeleştirilmiş* edition is rewritten in modern words; a transcription keeps the author's language.
